title: Distributed computation to useful output
scope: Four additive lessons closing specific semantic bridges in existing compiler, collective, training and decoding coverage. Existing curriculum, models and historical timelines are preserved.

chapters.name: Distributed computation to useful output
chapters.parent: Software / semantics, movement and accepted results
chapters.scale: One tensor or optimizer update to rank ownership and accepted tokens; logical diagram
chapters.title: Preserve the computation across its boundaries
chapters.summary: Reconstruct sharded matrix results, normalize uneven distributed gradients, inspect rounded reductions and verify speculative output.
chapters.question: When does completing communication also complete the intended computation?
chapters.read: Follow the worked values and declared numerical contract. Software boxes denote dependencies and ownership, not physical layers or measured timing.

lessons.name: Sharded matrix multiplication and result ownership
lessons.role: Derive the communication operation from the partitioned matrix axis and the next consumer’s required result layout.
lessons.description: A compiler must preserve both a tensor’s values and who owns them. Splitting matrix output rows gives different ranks independent output rows; splitting the contracted inner dimension gives each rank only part of every output sum. Those are different meanings of a local matrix product, even if the local arrays have similar shapes. JAX’s explicit sharding example forms local products and then reduces their partial sums. A sum all-reduce makes the completed result available at every rank. Reduce-scatter instead finishes the sum while distributing different output pieces, and all-gather can later assemble those pieces when a consumer needs a replica. Concatenating unfinished partial sums does not perform their missing arithmetic. This distinction connects tensor-axis information in a compiler to the collective scheduled over the network. It also prevents allocating replicas merely because the preceding stage happened to use all-reduce. A valid next operator may consume distributed rows directly, while another needs a different layout and an explicit conversion. The example below uses exactly representable small integers; its equality does not imply arbitrary floating-point reduction trees are bitwise identical.
mechanism: Declare C = AB, the complete tensor shapes, stored element size and required consumer ownership before partitioning.
Split the inner dimension into disjoint sets Kᵣ; each rank receives matching columns of A and rows of B.
Compute Cᵣ locally. Each Cᵣ covers all output coordinates but contains only the products indexed by Kᵣ.
Add contributions with matching output coordinates. Use all-reduce for replicated C or reduce-scatter for completed disjoint output shards.
Retain row shards when the next operation can use them; all-gather only when the consumer requires the whole tensor.
Check every output against a separate dense reference, and count a sent payload once at its chosen link boundary. Input distribution, temporary buffers and protocol overhead are additional costs.

science.title: Inner-dimension partition preserves the sum
science.equation: Cᵣ[i,j] = Σk∈Kᵣ A[i,k]B[k,j]; C[i,j] = Σr Cᵣ[i,j]
science.explanation: The disjoint Kᵣ sets cover the contracted dimension exactly once. Each rank contributes to the same output coordinates.
science.assumptions: Exact real arithmetic or the small integer example; floating-point summation order can change rounding. No duplicated or omitted contracted indices.

science.title: Two-rank payload ledger
science.equation: Qreduce-scatter = 8 bytes/rank; Qall-gather = 8 bytes/rank; Qcombined = 16 bytes/rank
science.explanation: For this explicitly described two-rank, 2×2 float32-output schedule, each phase sends one two-element row per rank.
science.assumptions: Logical payload sent by each rank in this chosen exchange; excludes initial input placement, headers, retransmission, local reads/writes and actual collective implementation details.

lessons.engineeringExample: Use A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and B = [[5,6],[7,8]]. Rank 0 owns k=0 and forms C₀ = [[5,6],[15,18]]; rank 1 owns k=1 and forms C₁ = [[14,16],[28,32]]. Reduce-scatter with row ownership sends C₀ row 1 [15,18] from rank 0 to rank 1, and C₁ row 0 [14,16] in the opposite direction. Rank 0 adds [5,6]+[14,16]=[19,22]; rank 1 adds [15,18]+[28,32]=[43,50]. Each sends 8 payload bytes if elements are float32. If both consumers need all of C, all-gather exchanges these completed rows for another 8 bytes sent per rank. Both then hold [[19,22],[43,50]]. Total sent payload is 16 bytes per rank, 32 across the two senders; counting the matching receives again would double-count this network boundary. Concatenating the two original 2×2 partial matrices would create four rows and would leave their sums unfinished.
lessons.learningObjective: Reconstruct the same 2×2 product from inner-dimension shards, choose a collective from output ownership, and reconcile the two-rank payload ledger.
lessons.misconception: A shard can be an unfinished contribution to every output, not necessarily a disjoint piece of the finished output.

check.question: Each rank computed all output coordinates using a different half of the contracted dimension. Is concatenating those local arrays enough?
options: No: matching coordinates still require a sum
Yes: more rows complete the dot products
Yes: any collective performs the missing multiplication
check.explanation: The local arrays are partial sums over different k indices. Reduce them before choosing replicated or sharded ownership.

checks.question: After the stated reduce-scatter, which row belongs to rank 1?
checks.explanation: Rank 1 combines both partial contributions to the second output row.

checks.question: How many payload bytes are sent across both ranks in the two stated phases?
checks.explanation: Two ranks each send 8 bytes in each of two phases. The same received bytes are not added again.

lessons.whyAI: Distributed linear layers become correct only when the compiler and runtime finish the same tensor operation and deliver its expected ownership. Avoiding an unnecessary replica can also save memory and communication.
lessons.tradeoff: A shard-preserving collective may save result replication, but a later consumer can reintroduce an all-gather or resharding cost. Logical bytes alone do not predict network latency.
lessons.evidenceNotes: The sources establish sharding and collective semantics. All matrices, the two-row exchange schedule and byte counts here are synthetic. This is not an observed NCCL implementation, a topology model or a performance comparison.

lessons.name: Uneven batches and the global gradient
lessons.role: Preserve the intended training objective when ranks contribute different numbers of valid examples or tokens.
lessons.description: A synchronized gradient can be consistent across replicas and still represent the wrong objective. Suppose the intended loss is the mean over all valid training items in one optimizer update. A rank that averages two items and a rank that averages six have already divided by different denominators. Averaging their two gradient means assigns the smaller batch more influence per item. The global item mean instead weights each local mean by its valid-item count. PyTorch’s pinned DistributedDataParallel contract documents averaging gradients between workers, so the loss normalization and collective normalization must be considered together. The count can mean examples, unmasked target tokens or a sum of explicit sample weights; choosing it is part of the objective, not a hardware detail. This lesson derives one scalar update from a concrete squared-error loss. It assumes the same current parameter at both ranks and no cross-sample operation such as batch-dependent normalization. A rank exhausting its entire input stream is a separate synchronization problem: matching collective participation does not by itself fix per-item weighting.
mechanism: Define which items count in the loss and record their global count N for this optimizer update. Exclude padding only when the objective says to exclude it.
Compute local loss sums or local means and retain the valid count associated with each reduction.
For a rank-mean reducer over P active participants, scale a local mean gradient by P nᵣ/N before the averaging collective. Equivalently reduce local sums and divide once by N.
During gradient accumulation, use the count over the entire update window rather than silently averaging unequal microbatch means.
Apply the same synchronized gradient and optimizer state transition at every replica, then compare the result with the unpartitioned reference objective.
Handle empty local contributions and exhausted ranks with explicit participation rules; never divide an empty local mean by zero or simply omit a required collective.

interfaces.name: Per-rank loss contributions

interfaces.name: Global optimizer update
interfaces.signal: One correctly normalized gradient applied consistently

science.title: Global item-mean gradient
science.equation: N = Σr nᵣ; g = (1/N) Σr nᵣ ḡᵣ
science.explanation: Each local ḡᵣ is the mean of gradients for nᵣ valid equally weighted items. Multiply by nᵣ to recover the local sum.
science.assumptions: N>0, same parameters and differentiable separable per-item loss. No cross-sample dependence; sample weights replace counts when the objective uses unequal weights.

science.title: Compensate a mean-across-ranks reducer
science.equation: g = (1/P) Σr [(P nᵣ/N) ḡᵣ]; wnew = w − ηg
science.explanation: The factor P nᵣ/N ensures the subsequent division by P leaves the intended global item mean.
science.assumptions: P fixed participating ranks for this update; no custom reducer scaling. The scalar SGD update has no momentum, clipping, weight decay or loss scaling.

lessons.engineeringExample: Take ℓ(w;y)=½(w−y)² at w=10. Rank 0 has targets [9,9], producing gradients [1,1], count 2 and mean 1. Rank 1 has [7,7,7,7,7,7], producing six gradients of 3, count 6 and mean 3. The unpartitioned objective has gradient (2×1+6×3)/8=2.5. Averaging rank means gives (1+3)/2=2 instead. With learning rate 0.1, correct SGD gives wnew=9.75; the unweighted rank mean gives 9.8. For a reducer that divides by P=2, scale the local means by 2×2/8=0.5 and 2×6/8=1.5. It then averages 0.5 and 4.5 to obtain 2.5. If the ranks each held four valid items, equal weighting would be appropriate. Token-level training needs the valid target-token count when that is the declared loss denominator; sequence counts need not be proportional.
lessons.learningObjective: Derive and test a globally normalized gradient from unequal local batch means, then distinguish objective equivalence from replica synchronization.
lessons.misconception: A mean across ranks is a mean across training items only when local denominators and weights make it so.

check.question: Two ranks have counts 2 and 6 and mean gradients 1 and 3. What is the global item-mean gradient?
check.explanation: The weighted numerator is 2×1+6×3=20 across eight items, so the result is 2.5.

checks.question: A mean-across-two-ranks reducer receives local means. Which scale factors preserve the eight-item objective?
checks.explanation: Scaling by P nᵣ/N gives 0.5 and 1.5; the reducer then averages 0.5 and 4.5.

checks.question: Does equal synchronized state prove the chosen sample weights were correct?
options: Only if the network is fast
checks.explanation: All replicas can agree on the same incorrectly normalized gradient.

lessons.whyAI: The number of completed updates is useful only relative to the training objective those updates optimize. Ragged data, masking and uneven accumulation can change that objective through an unnoticed denominator.
lessons.tradeoff: Keeping exact counts and a reference objective adds bookkeeping and sometimes a small count reduction. It prevents an apparent scaling improvement from silently changing sample influence.
lessons.evidenceNotes: The PyTorch source is pinned to v2.8.0 and supports the default averaging convention, not a claim about every backend or custom hook. The squared-error data, gradient weighting derivation and SGD step are authored examples. Join semantics after input exhaustion are outside this fixed-participant update.

lessons.name: Floating-point reductions and compiler permissions
lessons.shortName: The order of a floating-point sum
lessons.role: Distinguish algebraic equivalence, numerical error and bitwise reproducibility when compilation or collectives regroup arithmetic.
lessons.description: Real-number addition is associative, but a floating-point implementation rounds intermediate results. Changing the reduction tree changes where those rounding steps occur. A compiler that vectorizes a sum or a distributed library that groups rank contributions differently can therefore produce different low bits, and cancellation can make the difference much larger relative to the final result. LLVM exposes reassociation as an explicit fast-math permission; permission to contract a multiply and add is a separate choice. Such options should be read as part of the numerical contract, not assumed to be enabled in every program. A fixed reduction schedule can improve repeatability without establishing that its answer is the most accurate. Conversely, a numerically acceptable answer need not be bitwise identical to another legal result. The small integer schedules elsewhere in the atlas deliberately avoid this issue by keeping every operation exactly representable. This lesson changes that arithmetic assumption while keeping the underlying sum visible.
mechanism: Specify input representation, accumulator dtype, rounding mode and treatment of fused operations before comparing outputs.
Write out the intermediate additions imposed by the chosen serial, vector or distributed reduction order.
Round after each stated operation rather than rounding only the final real-number sum.
Inspect compiler reassociation and contraction permissions, plus the library and rank topology that determine the actual reduction tree.
Compare with an independent higher-precision or exact reference where available; use an absolute tolerance near cancellation and a justified relative tolerance elsewhere.
Validate downstream loss or task behavior separately. A repeatability check and a numerical-accuracy check answer different questions.

specs.context: Does not guarantee identical rounded intermediates.

science.title: Rounding makes grouping observable
science.explanation: fl denotes one rounding to the specified floating-point format. Intermediate representability determines the result.
science.assumptions: The example uses finite binary32 values with round-to-nearest, ties-to-even; no underflow, overflow, NaNs, stochastic rounding or fused multiply-add.

science.title: Spacing at the chosen magnitude
science.explanation: In the binary32 interval [2²⁴,2²⁵), adjacent representable values are two apart. The halfway sum 2²⁴+1 rounds to the even lower significand.
science.assumptions: ULP here means the spacing immediately above 2²⁴. Spacing immediately below that power of two is 1; it is not constant across the boundary.

lessons.engineeringExample: Let a=16,777,216=2²⁴, b=1 and c=−16,777,216, all representable in binary32. Group left: a+b is exactly 16,777,217 before rounding, halfway between representable 16,777,216 and 16,777,218. Ties-to-even gives 16,777,216; adding c then gives 0. Group right: b+c=−16,777,215 is representable, so adding a gives 1. The exact mathematical sum is 1. A deterministic left reduction repeats 0 and is reproducible, yet its absolute error is 1. A hypothetical acceptance condition |computed−reference|≤0.01 rejects 0 and accepts 1. That tolerance is an authored condition for this example, not an accuracy threshold for real training. Accumulating these three binary32 inputs with sufficiently precise binary64 additions produces 1; this does not guarantee that wider accumulation always eliminates error in larger problems.
lessons.learningObjective: Reproduce both binary32 reduction orders and explain why compiler permissions, accuracy checks and reproducibility requirements must be specified separately.
lessons.misconception: Bitwise repeatability does not prove closeness to the exact result, and algebraic equivalence does not prove bitwise identity.

check.question: With binary32 ties-to-even rounding, what is fl(fl(2²⁴+1)−2²⁴)?
check.explanation: The first addition rounds back to 2²⁴ because adjacent representable values above it are two apart; subtraction then cancels to zero.

checks.question: Why does grouping 2²⁴+(1−2²⁴) instead give 1?
options: The network repairs all numerical errors
checks.explanation: Below this power-of-two boundary the required integer is representable, so no information is lost in the inner sum.

checks.question: Which evidence shows a result is accurate relative to a stated reference?
options: Only repeating the same bit pattern
An error check against the independent reference
checks.explanation: Repeatability and rank count do not establish numerical accuracy.

lessons.whyAI: Gradient reductions, attention sums and low-precision accumulations connect compiler decisions to optimization and model outputs. A faster schedule must still satisfy a declared numerical and task-quality contract.
lessons.tradeoff: Stricter ordering or wider accumulation can constrain transformations and consume resources. Their value depends on the actual error and reproducibility requirements; this example provides no throughput ranking.
lessons.evidenceNotes: The NVIDIA guide supports finite-precision nonassociativity, and LLVM specifies the cited optimization permissions. The exact operands, intermediate values and 0.01 tolerance are authored. Tests use binary32 conversions locally and do not constitute a GPU, compiler or multi-rank experiment.

lessons.name: Speculative decoding: proposals and verified output
lessons.role: Account for target-distributed output tokens while separating draft work, verification and actual elapsed time.
lessons.description: A draft model can propose several next tokens cheaply, but proposals are not yet accepted output. In strict speculative sampling, the target model evaluates the relevant conditional distributions and verifies the draft sequence in order. A proposal is accepted with a probability determined by the target-to-draft probability ratio. The first rejected position is corrected using the positive residual between the two distributions, and later proposals from that speculative branch are discarded. When all proposals are accepted, one additional target token can be emitted. This procedure preserves the target sampling distribution under its stated assumptions; it does not establish factual truth or force the same sampled text from the same random seed. The benefit can come from evaluating several target positions together and reusing data movement, while draft work, rejected work and additional state still consume resources. The exact three-symbol example below checks the sampling correction before considering a separately assumed timing budget.
mechanism: Use target p and draft q distributions over the same token events and the same valid prefix, including any declared sampling transforms.
Sample a proposal x from q; when q(x)>0, accept it with probability min(1,p(x)/q(x)). A symbol with q(x)=0 cannot be proposed.
After the first rejection, sample a correction from normalized max(p−q,0) at that prefix and discard the later speculative branch.
If all γ proposals are accepted, draw the extra token from the target distribution conditioned on the full accepted prefix.
Count accepted prefix tokens plus the one correction or bonus token as output; count draft proposals and rejected target work separately.

Measure draft, target-verification, synchronization and state-management time on the actual workload before claiming a speedup. Distributional equivalence remains separate from factual or task correctness.

specs.context: Ideal strict correction; not a guarantee of the same random sample or true statements.

specs.label: Output per verification
specs.value: 1 through γ+1 tokens before stopping rules
specs.context: Accepted prefix plus a correction or a target bonus.

specs.label: Resource boundary

interfaces.name: Aligned target and draft distributions

interfaces.name: Verified continuation

science.title: Acceptance and rejection correction
science.explanation: For a proposed symbol, accept with a(x). After a rejection, sample from residual r. Total acceptance probability is α=Σx min(p(x),q(x)).
science.assumptions: Finite normalized distributions with q(x)>0 for a proposed x. Use r only when its denominator is positive; if p=q no rejection occurs. Exact probability arithmetic and consistent prefixes are assumed.

science.title: Output count in the iid acceptance scenario
science.equation: E[K] = Σj=0…γ αʲ; Rscenario = E[K]/(Tdraft + Tverify + Toverhead)
science.explanation: K counts output tokens, including the correction or bonus. With iid acceptance probability α and no early stopping, the probability of accepting at least j proposals is αʲ.
science.assumptions: The iid assumption is synthetic; actual acceptance varies with prefix. Time terms are separately declared seconds per verification round; no measured speedup, energy reduction or universal latency scaling is implied.

lessons.engineeringExample: For symbols A/B/C, choose target p=[0.6,0.3,0.1] and draft q=[0.2,0.3,0.5]. Conditional acceptance is [1,1,0.2], so accepted probability mass is [0.2,0.3,0.1] and total α=0.6. The rejected mass is 0.4; normalized positive residual p−q is [1,0,0], so every correction in this toy case is A. The final output distribution is [0.2,0.3,0.1]+0.4×[1,0,0]=[0.6,0.3,0.1], exactly the target distribution. If γ=2 and acceptance events are independently 0.6 at both positions, output counts 1,2,3 have probabilities 0.4,0.24,0.36. Thus E[K]=1.96 tokens. Separately assume the two draft steps together take 2 ms, target verification 6 ms and overhead 1 ms: 1.96/0.009≈217.8 output tokens/s. A 6 ms single-token baseline would be 166.7 tokens/s under those assumptions. At 12 ms verification, the speculative scenario instead gives 130.7 tokens/s. Neither timing is measured or taken from the paper; acceptance alone does not establish acceleration.
lessons.learningObjective: Recover the target distribution by exact probability accounting, then calculate output-per-round and a conditional throughput without treating proposals or assumptions as measured useful output.
lessons.misconception: Accepting a draft token validates it against a sampling distribution, not against external facts; higher acceptance does not by itself prove lower latency.

check.question: In the stated toy distributions, a rejected proposal must be corrected from which distribution?
check.explanation: The positive residual is [0.4,0,0], which normalizes to [1,0,0]. Adding its weighted contribution recovers the target probabilities.

checks.question: Under iid α=0.6 with two proposals, what is the expected output count including correction or bonus?
Does preserving p establish that sampled statements are true?
checks.explanation: The target distribution can assign probability to factually wrong continuations.

lessons.whyAI: Useful serving throughput counts the output that survives the verification algorithm and meets the task’s quality requirements. This connects decoding semantics, memory reuse and latency accounting.
lessons.tradeoff: More proposals can expose useful parallel verification while increasing draft computation, temporary state and wasted work. Prefix-dependent acceptance and workload-specific target cost determine the result.
lessons.evidenceNotes: The cited ICML paper establishes the strict correction algorithm and the explicitly iid output-count formula. The toy probabilities, output-count distribution and all millisecond values are authored. No private model, serving implementation, benchmark speedup or quality improvement is asserted.
